{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Alan J. Goldman''' (1932–2010) was an American expert in [[operations research]].<ref name="nap">{{citation|url=https://www.nap.edu/read/18477/chapter/22|title=Alan J. Goldman 1932–2010|journal=Memorial Tributes of the National Academies|volume=17|year=2013|pages=122–126|first1=Daniel Q.|last1=Naiman|first2=Christoff|last2=Witzgall}}.</ref><ref name="jhu">{{citation|journal=The JHU Gazette|publisher=Johns Hopkins University|date=March 1, 2010|title=Alan J. Goldman, 77, expert in operations research|url=http://archive.gazette.jhu.edu/2010/03/01/alan-j-goldman-77-expert-in-operations-research/|archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20170503211020/http://archive.gazette.jhu.edu/2010/03/01/alan-j-goldman-77-expert-in-operations-research/|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 3, 2017}}.</ref>

==Career==
Goldman was born in 1932 and grew up in [[Brooklyn]], where his parents both worked for the public school system. In 1949, he was a winner of the [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]]. He studied mathematics and physics at [[Brooklyn College]], graduating in 1952.<ref name="nap"/><ref name="jhu"/>
He went on to graduate study in mathematics at [[Princeton University]], completing his doctorate in [[topology]] in 1957 under the supervision of [[Ralph Fox]].<ref name="mg">{{mathgenealogy|id=6732}}</ref>
Goldman worked at the [[National Bureau of Standards]] from 1956 until 1979, when he became a professor of mathematical sciences at [[Johns Hopkins University]]. He retired in 1999.<ref name="nap"/><ref name="jhu"/>

While at Princeton, Goldman came under the influence of [[Albert W. Tucker]], with whom he published three "seminal papers" in ''Annals of Mathematics Studies'' on [[linear programming]] and [[convex polytope]]s. His work at the National Bureau of Standards included work on [[Optimal facility location|facility location]] for the [[US Postal Service]] and on [[transportation planning]]; he was also a mentor there to [[Jack Edmonds]] and [[George Nemhauser]].<ref name="nap"/> After moving to Johns Hopkins, his doctoral students included combinatorialist [[Arthur T. Benjamin]].<ref name="mg"/>

In 1976,  Goldman won the Gold Medal for Excellence in Service of the [[US Department of Commerce]]. He was elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1989.<ref name="nap"/><ref name="jhu"/>
